extracted.intended_audience: humor writers looking for places to submit short humor, satirical news, and funny personal essays
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide to markets that accept satire, conceptual humor, satirical news, funny personal essays, and literary humor, with notes on format, word limits, submission channels, and pay considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match your piece to the publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you submit to a publication, you should spend some time reading it to make sure your piece is a good fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorization is tricky and some markets fit more than one spot; read the publication to see tone, length, and formats they publish. "Reading what these sites have run before should give you an idea of the type of style they are looking for."

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand subgenre differences (satire/conceptual vs satirical news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire/Conceptual humor pieces depart from reality in some way and can take most formats; satirical news is formatted like a newspaper article (sometimes just a headline) and is a distinct format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you aren’t already familiar with short conceptual humor, spend time reading relevant sites. The page separates markets into Satire/Conceptual Humor Markets and Satirical News Sites to emphasize format/content differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the correct format for satirical news
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical news pieces are formatted like newspaper articles (and sometimes just headlines); many general satire sites do not accept this newspaper-parody format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target dedicated satirical news sites (examples given: The Onion [closed], Reductress, The Hard Times, Hard Drive, The Needling, Broadway Beat). Check each site's submission directions because general satire markets often exclude this format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe publication-specific word limits and format restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications often specify maximum word counts and format limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the list: Chortle accepts short pieces of 600 words or fewer; Weekly Humorist accepts satirical humor pieces under 1500 words; Business Insider runs short (600-word) personal essays. Always consult each market's submission guidelines for exact limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: For Medium: prefer submitting to publications (and understand pay/Bost policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medium hosts publications and self-published posts; submitting to established Medium publications can reach a wider audience and using the paywall may earn money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you put your piece behind the Medium paywall you have the potential to get paid; pay ranges vary widely (less than $1 to over $100 per piece). Pieces selected for Boost tend to make more, so submitting to publications that have Boost can be worth it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check whether a publication accepts open submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets accept open submissions; others (notably The Onion) do not take submissions on an open basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm via each publication's submission guidelines whether they accept unsolicited work and how/when they open submissions (e.g., Reductress opens quarterly and lists info for next openings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know submission channels and contact instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different markets accept submissions via different channels (email addresses, submission portals, specified forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The American Bystander (print and online) asks for submissions to submissions@americanbystander.org. Follow the specific instructions on each market's submission/guidelines page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect longer response times and submission windows for literary journals and prestige outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary journals sometimes only open for submission at certain times of year and can have longer response times; some high-profile sections (e.g., New Yorker Shouts) can take months to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for submission windows in the guidelines and plan accordingly; factor in longer waits when submitting to lit journals and prestigious magazines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target niche or topical publications for subject-specific humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Many publications have rubrics/audiences for specific beats (parenting, regional, theater, gaming, punk music) and will prefer pieces aligned with those topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Frazzled is parenting-focused; Scary Mommy frequently blends parenting and humor; Hard Drive focuses on video-game satirical news; Broadway Beat is for theater-based satirical news. Match subject matter and tone to the niche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider format variety (cartoons, poetry, essays) when selecting markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Some markets accept formats beyond short prose humor—cartoons, poetry, and other forms may be accepted where noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekly Humorist accepts cartoons and satirical humor pieces; some literary journals (e.g., Defenestration) accept many formats including poetry. Check each market for allowed formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use market research resources and follow other writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding markets can come from following humor writers, tweet threads, and aggregator resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends following humor writers you enjoy to see where they publish, using resources like Chill Subs and Twitter threads, and consulting the author's additional guides and e-guide for leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic expectations about payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments for humor pieces vary substantially and are often modest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Medium pay per piece varies widely (less than $1 to over $100, upper end uncommon). Many web publications pay little or nothing—research each market's pay policy before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage examples and pitch guides for essay markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal-essay markets often run funny essays; reading published examples and pitch guides helps craft submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists example essays (Business Insider, HuffPost Personal, Slate, etc.) and links to pitch guides—use those examples to model tone, structure, and hook for timely or personal-essay submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that some markets are print + online and may have different expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications that run both print and online editions may have differing formats, editorial standards, or pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The American Bystander is a print and online publication—check whether submissions are intended for print, online, or both and follow any separate instructions.
